::: {.tag-list} [K-Means Clustering]{.tag} [Unsupervised Learning]{.tag} [Multivariate Data]{.tag} [Standardisation]{.tag} ::: This activity uses a short self-report app to give every student a personal profile across six dimensions: **Speed**, **Risk**, **Structure**, **Ambiguity**, **Social**, and **Pattern** — covering things like how quickly they make decisions, how comfortable they are with uncertainty, and whether they lean toward independent or collaborative work. Once the whole class has a six-number profile, the instructor runs k-means clustering live to sort students into groups based on similarity — and if the room allows, students physically move to sit with their cluster, turning an abstract clustering output into something they can immediately feel and discuss. ## Demonstration ## Materials - The **Six Micro-Tests Score App** (download below) — each student needs a device to access it
```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE} library(downloadthis) download_file( path = "test.html", button_label = "Six dimensions test", button_type = 'success' ) ```

- A tool for students to submit their six scores (e.g. Google Forms, or directly via the app's "Copy CSV" button if you're collecting responses manually) - A stats package (R recommended) set up to run k-means clustering live - Optional: enough open floor space or movable tables for students to physically regroup by cluster afterward ```{r} ``` ## The Six Dimensions | Dimension | What it measures | |---|---| | **Speed** | Quick vs. careful decision-making | | **Risk** | Cautious vs. risk-seeking responses | | **Structure** | Preference for clear instructions and rules | | **Ambiguity** | Comfort with unclear situations | | **Social** | Independent vs. collaborative working style | | **Pattern** | Rule-based vs. intuitive thinking | Each test has 5 items on a 1–5 scale (with reverse-scored items handled automatically), giving a raw score from 5–25 per dimension, or a mean item score from 1–5. ## Step-by-Step Plan ### 0 (Pre-tasks) - Test the app yourself and confirm the "Copy CSV" function works as expected on your setup - Set up a submission form (or a shared spreadsheet) where students can paste in their name and six scores - Have your R session or spreadsheet ready with a k-means script prepared in advance (see Step 4), so you're not writing code live in front of the class ### 1 (Setup) Direct students to the app and explain the task: > "You're going to complete six very short tests, each with 5 quick questions. Just answer honestly and quickly — there's no right or wrong answer here. Give yourself 5 to 10 minutes to get through all six." ### 2 (Complete the Tests) Give students 5–10 minutes to work through all six tests in the app. Once finished, they click "Calculate scores" and then "Copy CSV" to get their six-dimension profile. ### 3 (Collect the Data) Have students paste their name and six scores into your shared submission form or spreadsheet. Compile the full class dataset — each row is one student, each column is one of the six dimension scores. ### 4 (Standardise the Data) Before running k-means, standardise each dimension so no single test dominates the clustering just because it happens to have more spread. ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Why standardise first? K-means clustering is based on distance between points. If one dimension has a much larger range or variance than the others, it will dominate the distance calculation and effectively drown out the other five dimensions. Standardising each column to a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1 puts all six dimensions on equal footing. $$ z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s} $$ ::: ```r scores_raw <- read.csv("class_scores.csv") scores_z <- scale(scores_raw[, c("speed","risk","structure","ambiguity","social","pattern")]) ``` ### 5 (Choose the Number of Clusters) Before running k-means, decide how many clusters ($k$) to use. A simple, visual approach for class purposes is the **elbow method**: plot total within-cluster variation against different values of $k$, and look for the point where adding more clusters stops giving a big improvement. ```r wss <- sapply(1:8, function(k) kmeans(scores_z, centers = k, nstart = 10)$tot.withinss) plot(1:8, wss, type = "b", xlab = "Number of clusters (k)", ylab = "Within-cluster sum of squares") ``` Discuss with the class where the "elbow" appears to be, and pick a $k$ that's small enough to be meaningful for regrouping the room (e.g. 3–5 clusters). ### 6 (Run K-Means) ```r set.seed(123) km <- kmeans(scores_z, centers = 4, nstart = 25) scores_raw$cluster <- km$cluster ``` Display each student's assigned cluster alongside their name. ### 7 (Interpret the Clusters) For each cluster, calculate the average (standardised) score on each of the six dimensions, and display it as a table or radar-style summary. ```r aggregate(scores_z, by = list(cluster = km$cluster), FUN = mean) ``` Ask the class to help name each cluster based on its profile — e.g. a cluster high on Risk and low on Structure might get nicknamed "The Improvisers," while a cluster high on Structure and Pattern might be "The Planners." ### 8 (Move and Discuss) If the room allows, announce each student's cluster and have them physically move to sit with their group. Once seated together, give each group a few minutes to discuss: - Do you feel like this cluster actually describes you? Why or why not? - What do you have in common with the others at your table, beyond just the six numbers? - Is there a dimension where your group is surprisingly *split*, even though you were clustered together overall? ## Bonus / Optional: - Can relate this activity to dimensionality and the curse of high dimensions - A few extensions to try: - **Visualise in 2D:** Run PCA on the standardised data and plot the first two principal components, coloured by cluster, so students can see a 2D "map" of the whole class. - **Compare k values:** Re-run the clustering with a different $k$ (e.g. 3 vs. 6) and discuss how the groupings — and the physical seating — would have changed. - **Hierarchical clustering:** Run an agglomerative hierarchical clustering on the same data and display a dendrogram, comparing which students get grouped together versus the k-means result. - **Stability check:** Re-run k-means a few times with different random starting points (`nstart`) and discuss why the algorithm can converge to different results depending on initialisation — a nice segue into why `nstart` with multiple restarts is standard practice.
